title: Caring for our world: litter, bins, water and lights

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 24 Nov 2026: litter harming animals (squirrels and hedgehogs trapped in cans and cartons, birds tangled) against RSPCA 'Litter' guidance; crisp packets not accepted in most UK household recycling while cans, paper and glass jars are, against WRAP Recycle Now item pages; food scraps to food waste for composting against WRAP; reuse ranked above recycling against the waste hierarchy in the Waste (England and Wales) Regulations 2011; a running bathroom tap at about 6 litres a minute against Waterwise, so 2 minutes of brushing wastes about 12 litres, matching the lab's 4 x 30 s brushes at 3 litres each; switching off unused lights and TVs saves energy and some UK electricity still comes from burning gas, against Energy Saving Trust and DESNZ Energy Trends.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets common early-years slips for NGSS K-ESS3-3 and KS1 environment work: shiny crisp packets go in recycling (step 2 predict and 'shiny' slip), food scraps belong in the rubbish ('food'), recycling is always best so a new bottle each day is fine (step 3 predict and 'recycle'), leaving the tap running while brushing does not matter ('tap'), all lights must go off even when someone is reading ('using' and the living-room refusal), and flowers or snails are litter to be tidied away (the 'flower' slip and refused Pick up buttons).

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanisms specific to caring for the environment: a park scene where each piece of litter is tapped into a bin and the animal it endangered is named as safe, with flowers and snails refused; a three-bin sorter for six real items with crisp packet refused from recycling; a refill-bottle versus new-bottle counter that grows a rubbish pile; a brushing timer with tap-on or tap-off that fills a litre bucket; and a four-room house where only empty-room lights and TVs may be switched off. The gate measured under 30% overlap with every other flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing before the strip confirms it: the animal count falls as each piece of litter goes in the bin; the crisp packet bounces from the recycling bin with the reason; three refills leave no new rubbish while new bottles pile up; the bucket fills by 3 litres for every 30 s brush with the tap on and stays dry with it off; and the house refuses to switch off the living-room light while someone reads there, so learners discover 'only when nobody is using it'.

predictions.evidence: Two committed predictions before acting: 'Can a shiny crisp packet go in the home recycling?' (step 2) and 'Which makes less rubbish: a new bottle each day or one bottle you fill again?' (step 3). Show me cannot run until a choice is locked in, and the strip then says 'You predicted ... now you know why'. The tasks for steps 2, 3 and 4 also ask learners to act out a reason, not just tap.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles six concrete scenarios (can on the grass, crisp packet bin, refill bottle, tap while brushing, Grandad reading, flower in the park), rotating answer order each time. Every wrong pick gives a targeted reason through the matching slip ('Crisp packets cannot go in the home recycling, even though they are shiny...'), and every answer offers 'Next one' so children can keep practising.

readability.evidence: Family audience for ages 5-6: kid text grade 1.7 and adult text 7.6 against the family limits of 5.0 and 10. Lab strings use short words ('Litter left out can hurt animals. Put it in a bin.'), emoji pictures sit beside every label, and the Sound button reads each strip aloud for pre-readers.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact or an action: what litter does to named animals, which of three bins each everyday item goes in, why using again beats recycling, the 6 litres a minute tap figure, and the rule to switch off only empty rooms. The adult paragraphs name the crisp-packet and 'all lights off' mistakes and give one home routine to try. The content gate passed the filler and similarity checks.

mobile.evidence: Checked at iPhone 13 width (390 px) in light and dark themes: park, bins, bottle, bucket and house panels fit without clipping after moving the animals inward and enlarging emoji; all controls are full-width buttons at least 44 px tall; the bin and room cards are large tap targets for 5-year-olds; and every Show me finishes inside the 6 s walkthrough limit.

accessibility.evidence: Canvas has an aria-label plus a live text description that updates after each action (for example 'The juice carton is in the bin... Now the squirrel is safe.'). Every gesture has a button alternative (Pick up, bin buttons, Switch off the ... light), A.gest supports swipes, and colour is never the only cue: lit rooms show bulbs and labels. axe is clean in both themes in the walkthrough.

sources: NGSS K-ESS3-3: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air and other living things
DfE (2013) National Curriculum science, KS1 working scientifically and environment links; Early Years Foundation Stage, Understanding the World
RSPCA: Litter, and how it harms animals
WRAP Recycle Now: crisp packets, cans, paper, glass jars and food waste item guidance
The Waste (England and Wales) Regulations 2011: waste hierarchy (prevention and reuse before recycling)
Waterwise: a running tap uses about 6 litres a minute
Energy Saving Trust: switch off lights and appliances when not in use
DESNZ Energy Trends: share of UK electricity from gas
